text:
The Liberty & Society Student Fellowship is a selective, fully funded online program run by Australia’s Centre for Independent Studies (CIS). It is aimed at students and young professionals interested in free markets, individual liberty, public policy and the open exchange of ideas.
This is a sustained, discussion-based educational fellowship, not employment, a research appointment or a cash scholarship. The source describes it as ten months, with sessions listed from April to December.
What the fellowship involves
The published structure is:
- April through December
- 13 online sessions, normally every third Thursday
- 6:00–8:00 p.m. Sydney time
- Delivered through Zoom
- A seminar or presentation from a guest speaker
- Q&A
- Facilitated or group-based discussion
- A short written reflection after each session
- Three short oral reviews, or viva voce discussions
The speakers are drawn from academia, business, public policy and entrepreneurship. CIS says the program combines economics, political philosophy and applied public-policy discussion. Topics advertised include public choice, regulation and competition, artificial intelligence, energy markets, free speech, civil liberties, law, innovation and entrepreneurship. Official fellowship overview
Intellectual orientation
This is explicitly a classical-liberal program. Its organising ideas include:
- Individual liberty and responsibility
- Free markets and private enterprise
- Limited government
- Freedom of speech and association
- Property rights
- The rule of law
- Voluntary institutions and civil society
- Skepticism about regulation, state planning and political incentives
That does not necessarily mean every speaker or participant agrees with every CIS position. The session questions published for 2026 frequently invite objections, comparisons with social democracy and consideration of market failure or private power. But applicants should expect the program’s starting perspective and institutional culture to be strongly classical liberal and generally market-oriented.
CIS itself was founded in 1976. It describes itself as politically non-partisan and says it receives no government funding or commissioned-research funding. Its stated mission is to promote free choice, individual liberty, cultural freedom and open debate. CIS mission · CIS history
Eligibility
The CIS material indicates that the Liberty & Society programs are intended for:
- People over 18
- Applicants living in Australia or New Zealand
- Undergraduates, postgraduates and recent graduates
- Young professionals
- People from any academic discipline
High-school students are not eligible. No previous study of economics, politics or classical liberalism is required. CIS says it looks for intellectual curiosity, initiative and a willingness to engage seriously with competing ideas.
One small ambiguity is that the dedicated fellowship page does not publish a precise upper age limit. The separate Liberty & Society Workshop has an explicit 18–27 limit, but the fellowship page does not state that this same cap applies to fellows.
Cost and what “fully subsidised” means
There is no participation fee: CIS donors fund the program. Nothing on the published fellowship page indicates that fellows receive:
- A stipend
- A salary
- A research grant
- Academic credit
- Employment with CIS
So “fully subsidised” appears to mean that participation is free, not that participants are paid.
Workload and graduation requirements
CIS’s general page says fellows must:
- Attend at least 10 of the 13 sessions
- Submit the required written reflections
- Complete three viva voce reviews
Successful participants receive a certificate of completion.
The public pages contain two minor inconsistencies:
- The general page describes reflections as 200–300 words, while the live 2026 cohort instructions say 300 words.
- The general page calls each viva a ten-minute discussion, while the cohort hub says 15 minutes.
The cohort-specific hub is likely the operational authority for current fellows.
The 2026 instructions say reflections are usually due at 11:59 p.m. on the Thursday two weeks after the relevant session. Readings are encouraged but described as non-mandatory.
The viva voce and use of AI
Three times during the program, a CIS staff member selects one of the fellow’s written submissions and discusses it with them orally.
The 2026 hub says this serves two purposes:
- Encouraging fellows to explain and develop their ideas
- Checking that submitted work represents the fellow’s own thinking
The reported CIS policy does not prohibit AI use outright. Its published instruction says fellows may use AI, provided the thoughts and answer remain their own. The oral review is intended to test that intellectual ownership.
Participation rules
For the 2026 cohort:
- Cameras must remain on during sessions.
- Sessions are not recorded or uploaded.
- Discussions operate under the Chatham House Rule.
- Participants may use ideas from the discussion but may not identify who made a particular comment.
- Fellows beginning at the start of the program may miss as many as three sessions.
- The hub says participants entering through the Liberty & Society Conference may miss only two; this appears to reflect their different entry point or schedule.
- Additional absences require a medical certificate.
The lack of recordings and the Chatham House arrangement are intended to allow speakers and fellows to speak candidly. 2026 fellows’ program hub

Published discussion questions have included:
- Whether regulatory capture weakens the case for government intervention
- Whether capitalism is uniquely compatible with reason and individual rights
- Whether private economic power can undermine genuinely voluntary exchange
- Whether new universities should face lower regulatory barriers
- Whether income-contingent student loans are the least-bad higher-education funding model
- How industrial policy can avoid capture and political favouritism
- Whether economic growth can help solve environmental problems
- What government policies inhibit entrepreneurship
- When additional law can produce greater liberty
- Where the legal threshold for intervention against harmful speech should sit
The list shows that the course is not simply a sequence of abstract lectures: participants are expected to apply classical-liberal concepts to live Australian controversies.
Benefits after completion
Graduates enter the Liberty & Society Alumni Network. CIS advertises continuing access to:
- Professional and intellectual networks
- Internship opportunities
- Subsidised attendance at CIS events and conferences
- Priority access to other or advanced Liberty & Society programs
These are access opportunities rather than guaranteed internships or jobs.
Relationship to the Liberty & Society Conference
The fellowship should not be confused with the Liberty & Society Student Conference:
- The fellowship is online, lasts ten months and has continuing written and oral requirements.
- The conference is a short residential event with lectures, discussions, social activities and networking.
- The workshop is a separate one-day program focused on personal finance, investing and entrepreneurship.
Conference participants can apparently progress into the fellowship, and some 2026 fellows entered through the conference.
History and alumni
The broader Liberty & Society program dates to approximately 1996 and was begun by Andrew Norton, then a CIS editor and researcher. CIS reports that more than 1,000 people have participated in Liberty & Society programs.
CIS names Josh Frydenberg, Kelly O’Dwyer and former New Zealand opposition leader Simon Bridges among the broader program’s alumni. Historical CIS material also mentions Michael Keenan, Scott Ryan and founders of several Australian libertarian organisations.
A necessary qualification: these individuals are alumni of the wider Liberty & Society conference/program tradition. The supplied source establishes no evidence that they completed the newer ten-month online fellowship specifically. Liberty & Society programs
Applications
Applications for the 2027 fellowship are not yet open. CIS currently offers a non-binding expression-of-interest form; registering interest is not itself an application.
CIS describes admission as selective but does not publicly state:
- The cohort size
- The acceptance rate
- A detailed marking rubric
- Whether interviews are required
- The precise application questions
- A confirmed opening or closing date for the 2027 round
